claim: The findings rest on two samples of healthy adults: Study 1 (behaviour only, N = 40) and Study 2 (fMRI, N = 44), with the Study 2 sample size fixed a priori by a G*Power analysis and the fMRI data of four Study 2 participants excluded for excessive head motion.
evidence: Forty healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22–31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study), and 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23–50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study).
notes: The a-priori sample size (G*Power, d = 0.56, required N = 44) and the four head-motion exclusions are folded in here as components of the scope claim rather than returned as separate methodological claims.

claim: On each trial participants chose between a safe monetary option and a risky lottery, under three conditions: deciding for themselves (Solo), for themselves and the partner (Social), and for the partner deciding for both (Partner).
evidence: There were three kinds of trials: decisions by the participant only for themselves ( Solo  condition), decisions by the participant for themselves and the partner ( Social  condition), and decisions by the partner for both themselves and the participant ( Partner  condition).

claim: Study 2 reproduced the Study 1 design inside the fMRI scanner with otherwise identical parameters, except for longer inter-stimulus intervals (3–11 s) and a fixed experimenter partner.
evidence: In Study 2, participants performed two sessions of the experiment described above inside the fMRI scanner. All parameters were identical except that ISIs varied from 3 to 11 s (drawn randomly from a gamma distribution).

claim: A pre-task icebreaker game succeeded in establishing a positive attitude toward the partner: average partner ratings on sympathy, cooperativity, honesty, openness and sociability were all above 8 on a 1–10 scale in both studies.
evidence: Results of a brief questionnaire indicate that this approach was successful: participants’ average ratings of their partners in terms of sympathy, cooperativity, honesty, openness and sociability were all above 8 on a scale of 1–10, in both studies ( Appendix 1—table 11 ).
notes: Manipulation check on the social-context manipulation the guilt interpretation depends on.

claim: To hold the partner's behaviour constant across participants, the partner's decisions were simulated by an algorithm that always chose the option with the highest expected value.
evidence: In order to ascertain constant decisions by the partner, the partner’s decisions were simulated using a simple algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value; i.e., it selected the lottery if EV diff >0
notes: A design commitment the Social-versus-Partner comparison turns on: partner behaviour is fixed, so differences track the participant's responsibility, not the partner's choices.

claim: Momentary happiness was modelled with five computational models (Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility, and Responsibility Redux) sharing separate, exponentially decaying terms for certain rewards, expected value, and reward prediction errors.
evidence: All models contained separate terms for certain rewards, expected value for lotteries and reward prediction errors, with influences that decayed exponentially over trials. We ran five models

claim: Model selection among the happiness models used likelihood ratio tests comparing the Responsibility model pairwise against each of the other models.
evidence: To formally assess which of our models fitted the data best, we supplemented the AIC, BIC,  R 2  and adjusted  R 2  values reported in  Table 1  with a series of  likelihood ratio tests : we compared pair-wise the likelihoods of the  Responsibility  model given the data to the likelihoods of all the other models.

claim: In both studies the happiness regression with all three two-way interactions (Equation 10) fitted the data significantly better (p < 2e−5) than the simpler models without interactions, licensing the report of its partner-outcome × decision-maker interaction term.
evidence: In both studies, the model reported in  Equation 10  fitted the data significantly better (p < 2e−5) than the simpler models without interactions (higher total and adjusted  R 2 , see  Appendix 1—table 2 ), but not significantly worse than the model with all interactions (p > 0.5; tested with the ANOVA function in R).
notes: The guilt effect is read from this model's interaction term, so which model was selected is load-bearing.

claim: A model-based GLM (GLM2) entered the best-fitting computational model's variables — certain rewards, expected value, participant RPE, and partner RPE from participant and from partner choices — as regressors to locate brain regions reflecting them.
evidence: In addition, we created another GLM (GLM2) with regressors designed to identify brain regions whose activation reflected the variables of the best-fitting computational model (see above).
notes: The model-based fMRI results depend on this GLM being built from the winning computational model.

claim: A parameter-recovery procedure on synthetic data generated from each participant's estimated parameters showed the happiness-model parameters could be reliably recovered.
evidence: We then compared these new estimated parameters to the actual parameters from which the synthetic data were generated, as follows: For each parameter, we calculated the mean of each participant’s recovered parameters and regressed these means on the participants’ actual parameters (see  Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ). The results show that the estimated parameters could be reliably recovered from noisy synthetic data.
notes: Validates that the model-based interpretations rest on identifiable parameters.
